newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's Wulf-Mathies wants regional aid overhauled.
newsitem.headline: EU's Wulf-Mathies wants regional aid overhauled.

text.p: EU Regional Affairs Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies called on Wednesday for an overhaul of European regional, social and farm aid spending, and said aid should not be used to fatten firms for privatisation.

"We are going to look into the possibility of some kind of privatisation clause," Wulf-Mathies told Reuters at the close of a three-day conference to discuss reforms to a massive EU spending programme which has tried but failed to narrow a wide gap in living standards between rich and poor European Union members.
Britain's Conservative government exploited a loophole in EU law to give large EU grants to public utilities in the late 1980s only to privatise them shortly afterwards.
But this did not constitute a breach of EU rules, Wulf- Mathies recently told the European Parliament, because it was up to national governments to decide how they used the money.
The German commissioner told Reuters she wanted the rules changed to force member states who privatised infrastructure built with EU money to continue using it as originally intended.
Similar controls were needed on what governments in the 15-member EU bloc did with EU money destined for public sector projects designed to reduce poverty, she added.
"Investments you made for the poor...could be used to reduce taxes for rich people," Wulf-Mathies said, stressing that the EU had limited power to control what the member states did.

This week's conference -- at which 1200 experts from the EU and 10 east European countries seeking EU membership discussed a strategy for a massive new seven-year spending programme starting in 1999 -- revealed widespread support for a simpler, better targeted programme, Wulf-Mathies told a news conference.

Despite spending 170 billion ecus ($192 billion) between 1994-99 to help the poorer countries -- Portugal, Greece, Ireland and Spain -- catch up with their richer partners, the EU has failed to bridge the poverty gap.

Wulf-Mathies said she thought the new programme should concentrate on three targets -- the Union's poorest regions; industrial, urban and rural areas worst affected by unemployment and poverty; and education and training.
The new programme had to adopt a more integrated approach, she said, bringing together economic, social, education, agriculture and environment measures.
It must also be less bureaucratic -- at EU and national level -- and its decisions had to be more transparent.

Wulf-Mathies said she wanted to stop governments presenting as nationally funded initiatives projects to which the EU had contributed 50 percent of the financing, perhaps by witholding some of the money until the EU was visibly credited.
The EU is due in July to begin discussing how it will finance the new post-1999 programme. Wulf-Mathies said she would fight for a budget at least as large as the current one.
